It's interesting in the wake of this fear seeing the ways that fear has invaded my mind and caused much suffering. Because in this state, I suddenly feel these dense fears around having killed one of the dogs back at the house by having shut them out in the heat. Something logically disconnected from the events, but seemingly a rational explanation for the density of fear present. It makes me wonder how much of the past was obscured by these fears. The good thing, I'm facing it and acting in spite of it. I didn't stuff my face, masturbate, play video games, or indulge. I'm sitting here, silently, in the parking lot facing my fear. I'll survive today and I'll be stronger for it. I won't be a professional teacher today, but I will make progress.

This stress and anxiety I'm feeling, the re-potting stress, is something I keep thinking about. I think the greats of every philosophy have talked about this sensation, the discomfort of the unknown. I think the general idea is finding a way to remain at peace while this feeling here, rather than waiting for it to die out. I still haven't figured that out.
The only things I need to do between now and my other job is rest and recuperate. Nap. Eat. And once those are taken care of, I can decide if there's more I want to do.

Of all the things I tried this morning (rant, meditation/centering, eating,) the only thing that actually made me feel better about the rest of today was napping during my 30. Rest is still underrated. I think the primary factor here is that present exhaustion or present hunger gets projected onto the future. This premonition then weighs on me as if the future is overwhelming and impossible. I hold onto such a notion until rest is achieved because I still have yet to understand how healing 3 hours can be. Or more likely, the future has little to do with why I'm actually feeling the exhaustion and is just a way of justifying the present truths. 

If exhaustion is present, sleep is a priority. Right now pushing through it to either work or indulge or practice is the priority, but I'd like to see it more taken care of. If hunger is present, food should be a priority. In either case, preemptive measures are far more critical. 

When is it hunger? When is it thirst? When is it sleep? When is it rest?

The week started out moving Joe from is apt in Kennesaw back to the house. Four of us, living at home again. It was a rough move, but one I felt stoic in. I spent little time falling into the arguments my mom had laid traps for, and instead got to work with packing, moving, then unpacking while the rest of them took care of the apt. It was bittersweet, because I could see how worried Joe was. He's experiencing what I went through three years ago and I have a lot of compassion for him. The rest of the week led up to a vacation with Taylor and friends. Throughout the week, I'd contemplated Taoism and Stoicism frequently. One concept which marinated throughout the week was in making room for growth to be natural, which id interpreted as taking care of my "soil." Because of this, I'd re-energized frequently via meditations (one lasting 45 min,) eating better, and sleeping more. Also making more room in my schedule and routine as a means of creating headroom. The result had me acting more diligent than I'd been in a long while. It left me contemplating the nature of thought and my own addiction, using thinking as a means of procrastination and prioritizing it over genuine joys like socializing. A recurring theme of the week was creating room for the natural, and how habitual moderation lets indulgence feel amazing when it happens. That and secure socialization. The week wrapped up in Ginny Springs, where I'd spent much time in autotelic experiences with my friends. It felt like a true realization of the visions I'd been having, and I'm grateful of having gotten to experience this weekend through new lenses.

Edit this, I'm too tired to make it sound real. But I also wanted to include a lot of how I've been prioritizing the joy of labor over any outcome, and how my own drive just to love the work is doing more than any other effort. At the same time, there's a deeper understanding of what it means to motivate others, and it all is just a symptom of taking care of yourself first.

On the ride up from Ginny Springs, realized it can somewhat be a waste of time listening to audiobooks *about* jazz. Why not...listen to jazz? I hardly enjoyed the book anyway, and felt much more joy listening to Horace Silvers instead of theorizing about him. That said the book did turn me onto him.
